DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The paper is clear and the core arithmetic is correct. However, it has **one factual error that undermines a proposal** and **one major omission that overstates the financial benefit by about a third**. The owners would be approving the plan on numbers that don't hold.

## Major issues

### 1. The risotto rationale is the reverse of what Table 1 shows (§5.2)

The paper says risotto "has the weakest margin on the menu." Table 1 shows it has the **strongest**:

| Dish | Gross margin % | Cash margin per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** (highest) | £11.20 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | **60%** (lowest) | £15.60 |

Risotto earns more cash per plate than the curry or burger. Its sales (90 a week) are only tied for lowest, with specials. Low volume may still justify a change, but the margin argument should be removed. The replacement special also has no stated food cost, so it could easily earn less. If risotto is the only standing vegetarian main, that is a separate risk worth noting.

### 2. The beef cost increase is ignored in the projections (§4 vs §5.3)

Section 4 reports a 12% beef increase from 1 April, the same day the new prices start. Section 5.3 assumes food costs stay flat. Treating the burger and steak as beef dishes:

| | Burger | Steak |
|---|---|---|
| Food cost now → after 1 April | £4.20 → £4.70 | £10.40 → £11.65 |
| Extra cost per week | £131 | £150 |
| Margin per plate gained, after cost rise | +£0.50 (not £1.00) | +£0.75 (not £2.00) |
| Gross margin % at new price | 70.6% (**down** from 72%) | 58.4% (**down** from 60%) |

The effect on the totals:

- **Net gain is about £529 a week, or £27,500 a year**, not £810 and £42,120. That is about 35% lower.
- **Main-course margin stays at about 70%** rather than rising to 71%. If specials are included at their 64%, it is roughly flat at about 69%. The claim that this "helps restore our 70% overall target" isn't supported.
- For the beef dishes, the price rises mostly just absorb the supplier increase.

The recommendation's "about £42,000 a year" and "improve our margin" (§8) need to be revised to match.

### 3. Check the VAT treatment

The margins appear to be calculated on menu prices that include VAT. If so, each £1 increase brings in only about £0.83 of net revenue, and all the margins are overstated. That would cut the £810 a week to about £675 before the beef adjustment. If the calculation is already ex-VAT, the paper should say so.

## Moderate issues

### 4. "Volumes will hold" is asserted, not tested (§5.3, §7)

- The evidence is thin. The 2024 change "had no visible effect on bookings," but bookings aren't plates sold, and no figures are given.
- A 60% repeat-guest rate means more customers will *notice* the change. It doesn't show they won't react.
- **Break-even volume losses** (the volume drop at which the change earns nothing extra), including the beef cost rise:
  - Fish and chips: about 8%
  - Burger: about 4.4%
  - Steak: about 4.6%

The burger and steak increases have very little margin for error, so a simple sensitivity table (for example, volumes down 0%, 5% and 10%) would strengthen the paper.

### 5. The monitoring plan can't separate price effects from seasonality (§6)

Comparing April–May sales with January–February will mostly measure the seasonal pickup. Better comparisons would be:

- the same weeks in 2025, or
- the unchanged dishes (curry, risotto replacement) as a control.

## Minor issues

- **Trading days:** §8 says "six trading days a week," but §2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- **Specials:** they are 9% of plates but have no price or cost shown, so the "main-course margin" figure can't be checked.
- **Competitor claims check out:** all three new prices sit below the competitor midpoints (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50).
- **Price communication (§6):** not highlighting the increases is a reasonable choice. Staff should still have a short, consistent answer ready for regulars who ask, given how repeat-heavy the customer base is.

## Verified as correct

- All Table 1 margins
- Weekly plates total of 1,050
- £810 a week and £42,120 a year, as arithmetic on the paper's own assumptions
- The roughly 71% main-course margin, but only if food costs are unchanged

## Suggested revisions

1. Rewrite §5.2: correct the margin statement, and base any removal on volume and menu variety.
2. Redo §5.3 with post-April beef costs, and state whether figures include VAT.
3. Consider a larger steak increase to protect its margin. At about £29.00, it would still be under the competitor midpoint and would recover close to 60%.
4. Add a volume sensitivity table and break-even volumes.
5. Change the monitoring baseline to the same weeks of the prior year.
6. Correct "six trading days" to five, and update the headline figures in §8.

*Note: the paper is dated March 2026, so actual April–October results should now be available. If this review is retrospective, comparing those results with the projections would be more useful than revising the forecast.*
